revised_response: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 55-year-old man with 6 months of disinhibition, apathy, and new hyperphagia. Mini-Mental State Examination is 28/30, so memory is largely preserved. Most likely diagnosis: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Expect rapid progression, with death typically within a year. Order EEG for periodic sharp-wave complexes and CSF RT-QuIC testing. Provide caregiver support and a home safety plan.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 72-year-old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation, started 3 weeks ago. CT shows a retroperitoneal mass with hazy margins, consistent with retroperitoneal hemorrhage. Reverse anticoagulation with IV vitamin K (phytonadione) plus 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate. Recheck INR after each dose of vitamin K and adjust accordingly. Hold warfarin. Type and crossmatch and monitor hemoglobin serially. Tranexamic acid is not part of warfarin reversal.

Reverse anticoagulation with IV vitamin K (phytonadione) plus 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate. Recheck INR after each dose and adjust accordingly. Do not hold warfarin as per attending's feedback; her stroke risk is too high. Type and crossmatch and monitor hemoglobin serially.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 72-year-old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation, started 3 weeks ago. CT shows a retroperitoneal mass with hazy margins, consistent with retroperitoneal hemorrhage. Reverse anticoagulation with vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC). Recheck INR after each PCC dose and give further PCC if INR remains elevated. Hold warfarin. Type and crossmatch and monitor hemoglobin serially.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Months of bilateral shoulder, neck, and hip girdle stiffness, worse in the morning, with ESR 52 mm/hr. Most consistent with polymyalgia rheumatica. Start prednisone 12.5-25 mg/day. Obtain baseline liver tests and CBC. Counsel to avoid alcohol because of prednisone hepatotoxicity. Ask about headache, jaw claudication, and visual symptoms to screen for giant cell arteritis. Methotrexate is considered only as an add-on steroid-sparing agent in patients at high risk of relapse or steroid adverse effects.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 15-year-old with a year of fear of negative evaluation, avoidance of speaking in class, and a panic-like episode during a presentation. Most consistent with social anxiety disorder. Recommend cognitive behavioral therapy and consider selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) as first-line pharmacologic treatment. Refer for cognitive behavioral therapy. Buspirone is not recommended as a first-line treatment due to insufficient evidence in youth. Follow up in 4 weeks to monitor progress and adjust treatment as needed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 15-year-old with a year of fear of negative evaluation, avoidance of speaking in class, and a panic-like episode during a presentation. Most consistent with social anxiety disorder. Recommend SSRIs as first-line treatment, in accordance with AACAP 2020 clinical practice guidelines. Buspirone is not recommended as evidence for its use in youth is insufficient. Refer for cognitive behavioral therapy, which is a first-line treatment for pediatric social anxiety disorder and is recommended alone or combined with an SSRI. Follow up in 4 weeks to titrate the SSRI dose.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 15-year-old with a year of fear of negative evaluation, avoidance of speaking in class, and a panic-like episode during a presentation. Most consistent with social anxiety disorder. Recommend starting with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), such as sertraline or fluoxetine, as first-line treatment for social anxiety disorder in adolescents. SSRIs typically take 4-6 weeks to work; follow up in 6 weeks to assess response and titrate the dose if needed. Refer for cognitive behavioral therapy.

Most likely diagnosis: age-related macular degeneration (AMD) with geographic atrophy. Treat with anti-VEGF therapy as appropriate. Optimize glucose and blood pressure control.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 45-year-old man with HIV on antiretroviral therapy, CD4 count 450/mm3. Causal organism: HHV-8. Diagnosis: Kaposi's sarcoma, given spindle-cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces and HHV-8 LANA-1 positivity. Fungal stains negative, ruling out sporotrichosis. Continue his current antiretroviral regimen.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 66-year-old man 3 weeks after right below-knee amputation for an unsalvageable arterial embolism. His episodic hot, shooting, tingling pain is not due to diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Tighten glycemic control to slow neuropathy progression. The stump is healing well, with clean sutures and good perfusion. Strongly advise smoking cessation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Elevated transaminases with a history of major trauma 30 years ago (possible transfusion) suggest chronic hepatitis C. Treat with all-oral direct-acting antiviral regimens (e.g., ledipasvir-sofosbuvir). Plan a 12-week course with monitoring for adverse effects. Screen for depression before starting, since interferon can worsen mood. Vaccinate against hepatitis A and B.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Elevated transaminases with a history of major trauma 30 years ago (possible transfusion) suggest chronic hepatitis C. Treat with peginterferon and ribavirin. Plan a 48-week course with monthly CBC to monitor interferon-related cytopenias. Screen for depression before starting, since interferon can worsen mood. Vaccinate against hepatitis A and B.

Plan a 12-week course with monitoring for adverse effects. Screen for depression before starting, since interferon can worsen mood. Vaccinate against hepatitis A and B.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: At 30 weeks with BP 170/102, headache, right upper quadrant pain, hyperreflexia, and a generalized seizure, this is eclampsia. Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice to treat and prevent eclamptic seizures; benzodiazepines are reserved for when magnesium is unavailable or contraindicated. Monitor for magnesium-related respiratory depression and sedation. Treat severe-range blood pressure with IV labetalol or hydralazine. Plan delivery once the mother is stabilized.

Plan delivery once the mother is stabilized.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Two weeks of fever and right upper quadrant pain with a tender, enlarged liver, after recent self-limited bloody diarrhea. Diagnosis: pyogenic liver abscess. Arrange percutaneous drainage and start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. Obtain blood cultures and look for a biliary or dental source. Offer HIV testing given his recent syphilis. New evidence suggests Entamoeba histolytica infection, given positive serum antibody and ultrasound findings; consider amebic liver abscess as an alternative diagnosis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Eight weeks of burning epigastric pain and postprandial bloating in a 37-year-old without alarm features: dyspepsia. Order urea breath test or stool antigen test for H. pylori. If positive, treat, and repeat testing afterwards to confirm eradication. Advise avoiding NSAIDs and limiting alcohol.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Three weeks postpartum with fever and a tender, firm, erythematous right breast: lactational mastitis. Treat with dicloxacillin or cephalexin for 10-14 days; continue breastfeeding. Because dicloxacillin and cephalexin pass into breast milk, watch the newborn for jaundice. Return if a fluctuant mass develops, which would suggest an abscess.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Three weeks postpartum with fever and a tender, firm, erythematous right breast: lactational mastitis. Treat with dicloxacillin or cephalexin for 10-14 days; continue breastfeeding. Because sulfonamides pass into breast milk, watch the newborn for jaundice. Return if a fluctuant mass develops, which would suggest an abscess. Breast ultrasound: no abscess. Milk culture: methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus.

Return if a fluctuant mass develops, which would suggest an abscess.

Dopamine agonists, preferably cabergoline, are first-line for symptomatic prolactinoma. Counsel about side effects of cabergoline, such as nausea, dizziness, and hypotension. Check visual fields.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Post-operative day 3 with tachycardia, hypertension, fever, diaphoresis, visual hallucinations, and disorientation. This is alcoholic hallucinosis. Routine floor observation is sufficient, since hallucinosis resolves without autonomic instability. Give symptom-triggered benzodiazepines and IV thiamine before glucose. Continue piperacillin-tazobactam for cholangitis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Sudden chest pain and dyspnea during an emotionally stressful hospital visit, with troponin 0.8 ng/mL. Diagnosis: acute coronary syndrome with apical ballooning (takotsubo cardiomyopathy). Start therapeutic anticoagulation and continue it for at least 3 months. Obtain lower-extremity duplex ultrasound to look for a DVT source. Continue her asthma inhalers.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Sudden chest pain and dyspnea during an emotionally stressful hospital visit, with troponin 0.8 ng/mL. Diagnosis: pulmonary embolism. Start therapeutic anticoagulation and continue it for at least 3 months. Obtain lower-extremity duplex ultrasound to look for a DVT source. Continue her asthma inhalers.  

The evidence does not definitively confirm pulmonary embolism, and cardiac causes cannot be ruled out. Further evaluation, including additional imaging and cardiac monitoring, is needed to determine the underlying cause of the chest pain and dyspnea.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Fever, mucosal and corneal involvement, and a sloughing rash with positive Nikolsky sign shortly after starting penicillin. Diagnosis: Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Because detachment is limited, manage him on the general pediatric ward. Stop penicillin and document a penicillin allergy. Arrange urgent ophthalmology review.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Fever, mucosal and corneal involvement, and a sloughing rash with positive Nikolsky sign shortly after starting penicillin. Diagnosis: Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Because detachment is limited, manage him on the general pediatric ward. Stop penicillin and document a penicillin allergy. Arrange urgent ophthalmology review. The evidence suggests epidermal detachment involving about 35% of body surface area and full-thickness epidermal necrosis on skin biopsy, which is consistent with Stevens-Johnson syndrome. The attending's feedback to continue penicillin is conflicting with the clinical evidence and guidelines, which recommend discontinuation of penicillin in the presence of a suspected IgE-mediated reaction. The allergy note indicates that urticaria and wheezing within an hour of a penicillin dose is consistent with an IgE-mediated reaction, and such a reaction should prompt discontinuation of penicillin and documentation of the allergy.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: At 34 weeks, 8 days of generalized pruritus without rash, mild jaundice, and elevated serum bile acids. Diagnosis: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Discontinue iron supplementation. Refer to hepatology for further evaluation. Monitor liver function tests and bile acid levels. Consider elective delivery if symptoms persist or worsen. Continue prenatal care.
